Waiting by the Stump: Why Does One Success So Easily Become the Wrong Method?
A farmer lived in the state of Song.
There was a stump in his field. A running rabbit happened to crash into it, broke its neck, and died.
The farmer had not chased it or set a trap.
The rabbit simply landed before him.
So he put down his tools and kept watch beside the stump, hoping to get another rabbit.
No rabbit came again.
The field went to waste, too.
This fable is usually taken to mean:
Do not mistake chance for certainty, or dream only of getting something for nothing.
But it contains another warning worth taking even more seriously:
The farmer did not go wrong because he had failed.
He abandoned what he could keep doing because **he really had succeeded once**.
The first rabbit was real.
It was no figment of his imagination, nor a promise someone had invented for him. He genuinely obtained a result faster and more directly than through his everyday farming.
That is precisely the danger of success.
Failure forces us to look for causes.
Why was there no harvest?
What was wrong with the method?
Have conditions changed?
Success can all too easily close these questions early.
Once the result is there, the method seems to have been proved as well.
What the farmer saw was:
I was standing in this field, and a dead rabbit appeared beside the stump.
He went on to conclude:
As long as I stay here, more rabbits will appear.
What is missing between the fact and the method is an understanding of the cause.

The rabbit's fatal collision involved many conditions outside the farmer's control: why it was running, which route it took, how fast it moved, where the stump stood. These conditions happened to coincide and produced the outcome.
The farmer's presence was not entirely irrelevant.
Had he not been in the field, he might not have collected the rabbit in time.
But “being able to obtain an outcome” and “causing that outcome” are not the same thing.
He mistook his position as the recipient of a result for a method of producing it.
Learning from experience does require us to repeat what has worked in the past.
A method's past success is an important reason to keep using it.
So the story cannot mean:
No individual experience is reliable.
What happened in the past cannot help us in the future.
Success teaches us nothing.
The real questions are:
Which parts of this success can be established again?
Which parts merely happened by chance at the time?
What, exactly, did my actions change?

Farming cannot guarantee a good harvest every season, either. Weather, pests, and many other outside conditions affect the result. But between tilling, sowing, weeding, and harvesting there is at least a connection the farmer can keep taking part in.
Watching a stump is different.
He has discovered no relationship in the first incident that he can actively establish. He merely hopes that chance will return in exactly the same form.
This is more than laziness.
It is a misunderstanding of his own role in an action:
Mistaking the place where luck once arrived for an ability he already commands.
A single success is particularly liable to become an identity.
Someone happens to make the right decision under a particular set of conditions, and others begin praising their judgment.
One way of expressing something happens to win widespread approval, and the speaker believes they have found a method that will always work.
An organization survives a crisis through a temporary arrangement, then keeps reproducing it even after conditions change.
Success brings more than results. It brings reputation, resources, and the authority to say what happened and why.
That makes renewed questioning harder.
To admit that a substantial part of our success came from chance can feel like diminishing our own achievement.
To admit that the method suited only the conditions of the time means relinquishing the certainty we have gained.
So we protect the stump.
Not because it really will bring more rabbits, but because it has become proof that we were once right.
The Han Feizi places this story within a discussion of the changes between past and present.
Its criticism is this: using the ancient sage-kings' once-effective methods unchanged to govern a different people in the present is like watching a stump against which a rabbit once happened to die.
The point is not to disrespect the past.
Past successes were real, and ancient methods may have made sense under their original conditions.
The problem is that people often move straight from “It once produced good results” to “This form is right in itself, forever.”

But a method's effectiveness may depend on population, resources, technology, relationships, and the distribution of risk. Once conditions change, retaining only the outward movements no longer amounts to repeating the same method.
An institution that looks the same may now be serving entirely different ends.
What truly deserves to be inherited from a tradition, then, may not be the location of the stump.
It may instead be how people in the past understood the problems of their own world and established connections between actions and outcomes under the conditions they faced.
If we copy only the answers without confronting the questions again, fidelity to the past can become a refusal to learn.
The story also leaves us with a question about opportunity.
The farmer did nothing wrong in taking the first rabbit.
We need not reject an accidental benefit simply because it was unplanned. Many opportunities in life cannot be manufactured in advance.
The problem began when he allowed one opportunity to replace all his abilities.
He stopped farming, stopped doing what he could continually influence, and handed his future entirely over to a chance event that had once favored him.
An opportunity can change our direction.

An unexpected encounter may reveal a new job, interest, or relationship. Real learning does not mean pretending we designed these accidents. It means gradually building new abilities after chance has appeared, so that the possibility it opened need not depend forever on the same kind of luck.

If the farmer learned from the rabbit's route and set up a suitable fence or trap, the story would be different. He would then be studying the conditions and trying to turn chance into intelligible action.
But he changed nothing.
He merely demanded that the world give him the same gift again.
Nor should this fable be used to mock every kind of waiting.
Some things really cannot be obtained by trying harder.

Waiting can be part of action: waiting for a season, for someone's reply, or for conditions that are not yet ready. The issue is not whether a person pauses, but whether they still understand what they are waiting for.
Waiting with good reason adjusts to new information.
It knows which signs show an opportunity approaching and how long to wait before trying another method.
Waiting by the stump, by contrast, cannot be changed by any new fact.

If a rabbit does not come today, perhaps it will tomorrow. If none comes this year, perhaps one will next year. Once the first success has been taken as final proof, every later failure means only “I haven't waited long enough.”
Reality can never disprove such a method.
And precisely for that reason, it is no longer a real method.
We usually worry that failure will damage confidence.
Waiting by the stump reminds us of the other side:
Success can damage judgment, too.
It leads us to mistake a result for a causal explanation, presence for ability, luck for direction, and a once-effective form for a rule that can no longer be questioned.
Truly learning from success means more than celebrating it. It does not mean modestly crediting everything to luck, either.
It means distinguishing more accurately:
What did I genuinely accomplish?
What was accomplished jointly by others and the circumstances?
What was merely chance?
Which of these relationships can be established again, and what cannot be asked to repeat itself?
The farmer watches the stump because it once gave him an undeniable result.
But the more real the result, the more necessary it is to ask how it came about.
Otherwise, one stroke of luck can shut down learning more readily than a failure.
The first rabbit had already died there.
The farmer's mistake was not eating it.
His mistake was believing, from then on, that as long as he stayed faithful to that stump, the world owed him a second rabbit.

*Textual basis: the passage beginning “There was a farmer in Song” in the Han Feizi, “The Five Vermin.” After the fable, the original states its political argument: “Those who now seek to govern the people of the present with the policies of the former kings are all like the man watching the stump.” This essay accordingly distinguishes real success, the relationships that produce it, repeatable methods, and waiting for an accidental result.*
